import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 363

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/363](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363)
- [BaBe07] Bauer, Mark and Bennett, Michael A., *On a question of Erd\H{o}s
  and Graham*. Enseign. Math. (2) (2007), 259--264.
- [BeVL12] Bennett, Michael A. and Van Luijk, Ronald, *Squares from blocks of
  consecutive integers: a problem of Erd\H{o}s and Graham*. Indag. Math. (N.S.)
  (2012), 123--127.
- [Ul05] Ulas, Maciej, *On products of disjoint blocks of consecutive integers*.
  Enseign. Math. (2) (2005), 331--334.
-/

namespace Erdos363

open Finset

/-- A finite set of naturals is an interval of naturals. -/
def IsInterval (I : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b : ℕ, I = Icc a b

/-- A collection of intervals as in Erdős Problem 363. -/
def IsValidCollection (S : List (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  (∀ I ∈ S, IsInterval I) ∧
  (∀ I ∈ S, 4 ≤ I.card) ∧
  S.Pairwise Disjoint ∧
  IsSquare ((S.map (fun I => ∏ m ∈ I, m)).prod)

/--
Is it true that there are only finitely many collections of disjoint intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ of size $\lvert I_i\rvert \geq 4$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ such that$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$$is a square?

This is false: Ulas [Ul05] constructed infinitely many such collections.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos363.lean"]
theorem erdos_363 : answer(False) ↔ {S : List (Finset ℕ) | IsValidCollection S}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos363

findings.description: The definition never excludes 0 from an interval. Consequently, for every n : ℕ, the singleton list [Finset.Icc 0 (n + 3)] is valid: its interval has cardinality n + 4 and its product is 0, which satisfies IsSquare. I proved that these lists form an injective family, establishing the entire infinitude conclusion using only zero products. This is not just an issue with allowing one block: [Icc 0 3, Icc (n + 4) (n + 7)] also passes the definition for every n, with two blocks of size four.
findings.source_evidence: Bauer–Bennett [BaBe07], Introduction, quotes Erdős–Graham's original question as asking when the product “is a nonzero square in only a finite number of cases” (https://www.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/Erdos-Graham.pdf). Bennett–Van Luijk [BeVL12], Introduction, explicitly requires solutions in positive integers (https://www.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/BeVL-Oct18-2011b.pdf).
findings.suggested_fix: Add `(∀ I ∈ S, 0 ∉ I)` to IsValidCollection. Equivalently, require the total product to be nonzero, or require every interval element to be positive. Include the nonzero/positive restriction in the theorem docstring.

findings.description: Set.Finite is applied to all valid lists simultaneously, with neither their number of blocks nor their block sizes fixed. The cited primary sources ask about finiteness for fixed parameters. Even after repairing positivity, the Lean negative answer only asserts infinitely many collections overall; it does not require infinitely many collections for any one fixed number and tuple of block sizes. Finiteness of every parameter fiber is different from finiteness of their union.
findings.source_evidence: Ulas [Ul05], abstract and pp. 331–332, states the conjecture for fixed k and l and explicitly distinguishes Skałba's earlier result: “if we allow k to vary, the above conjecture is not true” (https://www.e-periodica.ch/cntmng?pid=ens-001%3A2005%3A51%3A%3A41&bot=1). Bennett–Van Luijk [BeVL12], Introduction, states the question “for fixed r ≥ 1 and {k₁, k₂, …, kᵣ}” with each kⱼ ≥ 4 (https://www.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/BeVL-Oct18-2011b.pdf). The website headline leaves these parameters implicit.
findings.suggested_fix: After repairing IsValidCollection's positivity condition, place the fixed parameters outside Set.Finite but inside the answer proposition. For example: `answer(False) ↔ ∀ ks : List ℕ, (∀ k ∈ ks, 4 ≤ k) → {S : List (Finset ℕ) | IsValidCollection S ∧ S.map Finset.card = ks}.Finite`. Here ks fixes both the number and sizes of the blocks. Equivalently, assert that some fixed parameter tuple has infinitely many valid collections.

reformulations.difference: Collections are represented by ordered lists rather than unordered finite collections.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every valid block has at least four elements, so it is nonempty. Pairwise disjointness therefore prevents repeated blocks. Forgetting list order has finite fibers (the permutations of a finite collection), and validity is permutation-invariant. Thus the set of valid lists is finite iff its unordered image is finite. Both the finiteness equivalence and permutation invariance were proved in /workspace/review/reformulations.lean. This validates the ordering choice, independently of the two findings above.

The exact linked proof compiles under the supplied environment and depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Empty collections, empty intervals, reversed endpoints, and repeated blocks were checked; none yields an additional defect. The reviewed problem file was not modified.

Updated the docstrings while retaining the verified solved status and formal-proof reference. The required compile command succeeds with only the permitted sorry warning; scratch checks reject the zero-product families and verify that the cited construction proves the corrected statement.

/-!

namespace Erdos363

open Finset

/-- A finite set of naturals is an interval of naturals. -/
def IsInterval (I : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b : ℕ, I = Icc a b

/-- A collection of intervals of positive integers as in Erdős Problem 363. -/
def IsValidCollection (S : List (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  (∀ I ∈ S, IsInterval I) ∧
  (∀ I ∈ S, 0 ∉ I) ∧
  (∀ I ∈ S, 4 ≤ I.card) ∧
  S.Pairwise Disjoint ∧
  IsSquare ((S.map (fun I => ∏ m ∈ I, m)).prod)

/--
For every fixed $n \geq 1$ and fixed sizes $k_1,\ldots,k_n \geq 4$, are there only
finitely many collections of disjoint intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$ of positive integers with
$\lvert I_i\rvert = k_i$ such that
$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$$
is a square?

This is false: Ulas [Ul05] constructed infinitely many such collections with $n=4$
and $k_1=\cdots=k_4=4$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos363.lean"]
theorem erdos_363 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ ks : List ℕ, (∀ k ∈ ks, 4 ≤ k) →
      {S : List (Finset ℕ) | IsValidCollection S ∧ S.map Finset.card = ks}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos363
